slides.title: A shell converts syntax into a resource plan
slides.eyebrow: A SHELL CONVERTS SYNTAX INTO A RESOURCE PLAN
keyPoints: Parsing decides what commands mean
Execution creates processes and descriptors
Malformed syntax should fail before side effects
slides.narration: A shell does more than split text at spaces. It interprets a small language, then builds a plan for programs, arguments, pipes, files, jobs, and waiting. For a command that writes to an output file, opening that file too early could truncate it even though a later quote is unfinished. Separate parsing from execution so invalid syntax can be rejected without touching external resources. An abstract command plan is data describing intended work, not the work itself. We can test that data with no children and no file changes. Only after the plan is valid should the executor acquire resources and launch the stages.

slides.title: Word boundaries carry meaning after quotes disappear
slides.eyebrow: WORD BOUNDARIES CARRY MEANING AFTER QUOTES DISAPPEAR
keyPoints: An empty quoted word is still an argument
A quoted pipe is data
Token kind must survive removal of quote characters
slides.narration: Compare a quoted vertical bar with an unquoted vertical bar. Both may have the text | after quote characters are removed, but only the unquoted operator connects pipeline stages. The lexer must retain a token kind as well as text. Likewise, echo followed by two quotes contains an empty second argument; dropping an empty text field would change what the child receives. These rules explain why a simple string split cannot grow into a correct shell merely by adding more delimiters. Define the supported quoting and escaping language, preserve its structure, and reject unfinished forms before deciding which executable to launch.

slides.title: Run a typed-token parser model
slides.eyebrow: RUN A TYPED-TOKEN PARSER MODEL
keyPoints: Words become arguments
A Pipe kind divides stages
No token launches a process
slides.narration: The demonstration starts after lexical analysis. Its input tokens represent print, a quoted pipe word, an actual pipe operator, and count. The parser groups Word tokens into argument lists and opens a new stage only for the Pipe kind. It prints stages=2, first arguments=2, and literal argument=|. Those lines prove that the quoted bar remained data instead of creating an extra stage. This is a parser model, not a complete lexer or shell. It intentionally performs no expansion, redirection, or execution. That narrow boundary lets us check syntax behavior without creating operating-system resources or accidentally executing teaching input.

slides.title: Redirection order changes the descriptor graph
slides.eyebrow: REDIRECTION ORDER CHANGES THE DESCRIPTOR GRAPH
keyPoints: Duplicate the destination that exists now
Later reassignment does not rewrite earlier copies
Keep redirections ordered in the parsed plan
slides.narration: This second program is a descriptor-relationship model using names instead of real descriptors. First it redirects output to file and then duplicates output into error, so both names become file. The other order first duplicates the current terminal output into error, then changes output to file. Error remains terminal. It prints file/file and file/terminal respectively. The model does not open or truncate any file. It shows why the parser must retain the written redirection order rather than collect redirections in an unordered set. Real descriptor duplication shares the referenced open-file relationship at that moment; a later reassignment of one descriptor does not retroactively retarget the duplicate.

question.prompt: Why does the second error destination remain terminal?
question.answer: The duplication happened before output was reassigned, so it copied the earlier terminal relationship.

slides.eyebrow: WORKSHOP · CONTRACTS AND EVIDENCE

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Separate parsing from execution. Validate the complete structure and only then allocate pipes or launch children.

slides.title: Background jobs
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A background job allows the shell to continue accepting commands while the job runs.
The shell still owns bookkeeping and must reap child statuses. “Do not wait immediately” is not the same as “forget the child forever.”
Background terminal access has special behavior under job-control rules.
A robust interactive shell must manage notifications, stopped jobs, and later foregrounding rather than assume every background process can freely read from the terminal.

slides.narration: This lexer supports spaces, single and double quotes, simple backslash escaping, and the operators | , < , > , and & . Its double-quote escape rules are deliberately simpler than a full POSIX shell. It performs no expansion, substitution, execution, or redirection. Companion listing: ch42/lexer.py The explicit active flag preserves an empty quoted argument. Without it, echo "" could be reduced incorrectly to a one-word command. Typed tokens likewise preserve the difference between a quoted vertical bar and an actual pipeline operator. The next stage would validate token sequences and produce a command tree. Only after that validation should an executor allocate pipes or create children. This is an example of a broader systems principle: make invalid plans fail before acquiring external resources whenever practical.

slides.title: A pipeline needs overlapping stages
slides.eyebrow: A PIPELINE NEEDS OVERLAPPING STAGES
keyPoints: Bounded pipes cannot store unlimited output
Launch the consumer before waiting for the producer
Close every inherited end that has no role
slides.narration: Suppose a producer writes more bytes than a pipe can hold. If the shell waits for that producer to finish before starting its consumer, the producer blocks waiting for space and the shell waits for the blocked producer. A pipeline is therefore a connected set of overlapping activities, not a list of programs to run to completion one by one. Descriptor lifetime also matters. An extra open write end can prevent a reader from seeing end-of-file even after the intended producer exits. Draw each stage's input and output ownership, then close all unused ends in both parent and children as the execution plan is realized.

question.answer: It can wait for a producer that needs a consumer to drain a full pipe before launching that consumer.

slides.title: Some built-ins must change the shell itself
slides.eyebrow: SOME BUILT-INS MUST CHANGE THE SHELL ITSELF
keyPoints: A child has its own process state
cd in a child cannot change the parent directory
Choose built-in execution context deliberately
slides.narration: Imagine implementing every command by creating a child, running the requested operation, and waiting. That works for many external programs, but not for changing the interactive shell's current directory. A child can change its own directory and exit while the parent shell stays where it was. Built-ins therefore require an execution policy based on context, not a blanket fork-everything rule. A built-in used inside a pipeline may have different requirements from the same command entered alone. Keep that decision visible in the command plan and tests. The distinction concerns which process owns the state being changed; it is not merely a performance shortcut to avoid launching a program.

slides.title: A job is more than one child identifier
slides.eyebrow: A JOB IS MORE THAN ONE CHILD IDENTIFIER
keyPoints: A pipeline contains several processes
Foreground ownership applies to a process group
Completion requires all relevant child statuses
slides.narration: A two-stage pipeline may finish its first child while the second is still writing. Reporting the job as complete when one PID exits would be wrong. An interactive shell tracks a job containing all its members, often organized as a process group. Terminal foreground ownership and terminal-generated signals then apply to the job relationship, not just one remembered child. The shell must regain the terminal after the foreground job finishes or stops. Background jobs still need status collection even though the shell accepts new commands immediately. Storing a vector of PIDs helps bookkeeping but does not itself establish process groups, terminal ownership, or safe launch ordering.

question.prompt: Why is waiting for one pipeline PID insufficient for job completion?
question.answer: Other pipeline members can still be running or stopped, so the job’s aggregate state is not determined by one child alone.

slides.title: Partial launch failure still leaves real resources
slides.eyebrow: PARTIAL LAUNCH FAILURE STILL LEAVES REAL RESOURCES
keyPoints: Track every successful child creation
Close descriptors on each failure path
An exec failure must not return to the shell loop
slides.narration: A pipeline launch can fail after some resources already exist. Perhaps the first child was created and the second fork fails. The shell must close its remaining pipe ends and apply a documented policy to the already-started child, then collect its status. A child whose exec fails must report that failure and end the child branch; returning to the ordinary interactive loop could create an unintended extra shell. These cases show why parsing and execution should remain separate and why the executor needs explicit ownership records. Failure handling is part of the launch algorithm, not an afterthought after the successful diagram has been drawn.

question.prompt: What is dangerous about returning normally to the command loop after exec fails in a child?

slides.eyebrow: CHOOSE A SHELL ONLY WHEN SHELL SYNTAX IS REQUIRED
keyPoints: A fixed helper can receive an argument vector directly
Shell expansion adds interpretation rules
Validate plans before effects
slides.narration: An application that needs to run one fixed helper often does not need a general shell at all. Supplying an argument vector directly preserves one argument containing spaces without asking another language to interpret quotes, pipes, substitutions, or redirections. A shell is appropriate when the product intentionally offers that language and its process-control behavior. The choice affects both correctness and exposure to unwanted interpretation. Our typed-token example belongs to the shell side of that boundary; it teaches language structure. In application code, first ask whether users actually need operators or whether their input should remain plain data passed to a known executable.

slides.title: Test plans before testing launched processes
slides.eyebrow: TEST PLANS BEFORE TESTING LAUNCHED PROCESSES
keyPoints: Reject empty pipeline stages
Preserve empty and quoted arguments
Then test ownership, waiting, and cleanup separately
slides.narration: Build the test suite in layers. Lexer tests establish that an empty quoted argument survives and that a quoted bar remains a word. Parser tests reject a leading pipe, trailing pipe, missing redirection destination, or a background marker in an unsupported position. None of those tests should launch a child. Executor tests then check descriptor closure, redirection order, partial failure, and collection of every child. Finally, interactive job-control tests cover terminal handoff and stopped jobs. This progression keeps a syntax defect from being confused with a process-lifetime defect. A small supported language with explicit limits is easier to maintain than accidental behavior advertised as a complete shell.
